standard_text: Understand that the probability of a chance event is a number between 0 and 1 that expresses the likelihood of the event occurring. Understand that a probability near 0 indicates an unlikely event, a probability around 1/2 indicates an event that is neither unlikely nor likely, and a probability near 1 indicates a likely event. A probability of 1 indicates an event certain to occur and a probability of 0 indicates an event impossible to occur. Identify probabilities of events as impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, or certain.

progression.narrative:
This standard is really one big number line from 0 to 1, and every task is a matter of reading a point on it. A probability is a number between 0 and 1, and three landmarks give the line its meaning: 0 is impossible (it can never happen), 1 is certain (it always happens), and 1/2 is equally likely (a dead-even chance). Everything else is 'how close to a landmark is this number?' -- close to 0 is unlikely, close to 1 is likely. So the progression starts by nailing the three anchors, because a student who cannot say what 0, 1/2, and 1 mean cannot place anything in between.

From the anchors the arc builds outward. Before a student can classify a real situation, they have to turn it into a number: the probability of an event is the favorable outcomes over the total number of equally likely outcomes. With that fraction in hand, they classify -- first from a described spinner or bag, then straight from a fraction, always by comparing the value to the benchmark 1/2. The final move is comparison: given two probabilities, which event is more likely? The one whose probability is closer to 1. The through-line we keep naming is 'where does this number sit between 0 and 1?' -- the count of red marbles never decides likelihood on its own; the probability out of the total does.

steps.rationale: The anchors of the whole scale: a probability of 0 is impossible, 1 is certain, and 1/2 is equally likely. If a student cannot read the three landmarks, nothing in between can be placed.

Before a situation can be classified it has to become a number: probability is favorable outcomes over the total number of equally likely outcomes. This is the fraction every later classification reads.
Apply the scale to a described spinner or bag: find the probability out of the total, then place it. This is where students must resist judging by the raw count of favorable outcomes.
Place a probability given directly as a fraction on the full five-word scale by comparing it to the benchmark 1/2 -- the At-proficiency core of the standard.

The Above-proficiency extension: given two or more probabilities, decide which event is more likely. The reliable rule is 'closer to 1 is more likely,' which overturns the intuition that a bigger denominator means a bigger chance.

skills.name: Write a part-out-of-whole fraction from a set of outcomes

prerequisite_skill.description: Write a fraction for a part of a whole set, with the total on the bottom.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: 5 of 12 marbles are green. What fraction of the marbles are green?

skills.i_do_script: A fraction tells you a part out of a whole: the part goes on top, the TOTAL goes on the bottom. Watch: a bag has 3 red and 5 blue marbles. That is 8 marbles in all, and 3 of them are red, so the fraction that are red is 3/8. The bottom is always the whole group -- count everything, not just the leftovers. If 3 are red, the fraction that are NOT red is 5/8, because 5 of the 8 are the other color.

canonical_error.pattern: Puts one part over another part instead of over the total
canonical_error.example: For 3 red and 5 blue, writes the fraction that are red as 3/5 (red over blue) instead of 3/8 (red over the 8 total)
canonical_error.why: The student compares one group to a different group (part-to-part) instead of to the whole. A part-out-of-whole fraction always has the TOTAL number of items on the bottom.

skills.item_template: A set with named parts; student writes the fraction for one part out of the whole total. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue marbles. What fraction of the marbles are red?
A spinner has 8 equal sections; 2 are green. What fraction of the sections are green?
A box has 4 pens and 6 pencils. What fraction of the items are pens?
A number cube has 6 faces, each with a number. What fraction of the faces show a number?
A bag has 5 green and 7 yellow tiles. What fraction of the tiles are yellow?
A jar has 10 marbles, all red. What fraction are red? What fraction are blue?

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- what is the WHOLE group here?
redirect_script.prompt: Count every item to get the bottom number (the total). Then the part you want goes on top -- red over ALL the marbles, not red over the blue ones.
redirect_script.praise: You put the part over the whole total -- that's a part-out-of-whole fraction.

vocabulary.definition: The top number of a fraction; the part you are counting.
The bottom number of a fraction; the total number in the whole group.
One possible result, like drawing a red marble.

worked_example_script.text: Write: a bag has 2 white and 6 black marbles. What fraction are white?
How many marbles are there in all? How many are white?
There are 8 in all and 2 are white, so 2/8. The total 8 goes on the bottom.
If the student writes 2/6, ask 'is 6 the whole group, or just the black ones? Count ALL the marbles.'
Your turn: 4 of 10 tiles are striped. What fraction are striped?

skills.name: Convert a fraction to its decimal and percent forms

prerequisite_skill.description: Rewrite a fraction as a decimal by dividing, and a decimal as a percent.

skills.i_do_script: A fraction, a decimal, and a percent are three ways to say the same amount. To turn a fraction into a decimal, I divide the top by the bottom: 1/2 is 1 divided by 2 = 0.5. To turn a decimal into a percent, I move the point two places right: 0.5 = 50%. Watch: 3/4 = 3 divided by 4 = 0.75 = 75%. This matters for probability because seeing that 3/4 = 0.75 tells me it is close to 1, while 1/8 = 0.125 is close to 0.

canonical_error.pattern: Writes the fraction's digits as a decimal without dividing, or moves the percent point the wrong way
canonical_error.example: Writes 1/4 as 1.4 or 0.14 instead of 0.25, or writes 0.5 as 5% instead of 50%
canonical_error.why: The student reads the numerator and denominator as decimal digits instead of dividing top by bottom, and mis-scales the percent. The fraction bar means DIVIDE, and a decimal becomes a percent by multiplying by 100.

skills.item_template: A friendly fraction; student writes its decimal and percent equivalents. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Write 1/2 as a decimal and a percent.
Write 3/4 as a decimal and a percent.
Write 1/4 as a decimal and a percent.
Write 1/8 as a decimal.
Write 1/5 as a decimal and a percent.
Which is closer to 1: 7/8 or 1/8? Use decimals to decide.

redirect_script.stop: How do we turn a fraction into a decimal?
redirect_script.prompt: The fraction bar means divide: top divided by bottom. 1/4 is 1 divided by 4 = 0.25. Then for a percent, move the point two places right.
redirect_script.praise: You divided top by bottom, then scaled to a percent -- three forms, one amount.

vocabulary.definition: A number written with a decimal point, like 0.75.
A number out of 100; 0.75 = 75%.
Equal in value; 1/2, 0.5, and 50% are equivalent.

worked_example_script.text: Write 2/5 as a decimal and a percent.
What does the fraction bar tell you to do with 2 and 5?
Divide: 2 divided by 5 = 0.4. Move the point two right for the percent: 40%.
If the student writes 0.25 or 2.5, ask 'did you divide 2 by 5, or just write the digits?'
Your turn: write 3/4 as a decimal and a percent.

skills.name: Classify the likelihood of an event from a probability of 0, 1/2, or 1
skills.i_do_script: Probability is a number from 0 to 1, and three values anchor the whole scale. A probability of 0 means the event is IMPOSSIBLE -- it can never happen. A probability of 1 means the event is CERTAIN -- it always happens. A probability of 1/2 means the event is EQUALLY LIKELY -- it has the same chance of happening as not. Watch: 'An event has a probability of 0.' It can't happen, so it is impossible. 'A probability of 1' happens every time, so it is certain.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the ends of the scale -- reads 0 as certain or possible and 1 as unlikely
canonical_error.example: Given a probability of 0, chooses 'certain' or 'unlikely' instead of 'impossible'; or reads a probability of 1 as 'likely' rather than 'certain'
canonical_error.why: The student has not anchored the endpoints of the 0-to-1 scale. A probability of 0 means NO chance (impossible) and 1 means EVERY time (certain); the number is not just 'small' or 'one outcome.'

skills.item_template: A probability of 0, 1/2, or 1; student picks impossible, equally likely, or certain. Multiple choice.

sample_items.stem: An event has a probability of 0. Which word best describes it?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 0 means no chance; 'certain' reverses the scale.

sample_items.stem: An event has a probability of 1. Which word best describes it?
An event has a probability of 1/2. Which word best describes it?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1/2 is the exact middle; an equal chance either way.

sample_items.stem: A bag holds only blue marbles. What is the likelihood of drawing a red marble?
sample_items.distractor_logic: No red marbles means it can never happen.

redirect_script.stop: What does a probability of 0 mean -- can it happen at all?
redirect_script.prompt: Anchor the ends: 0 means it can NEVER happen (impossible), 1 means it happens EVERY time (certain), and 1/2 is a dead-even chance (equally likely).
redirect_script.praise: You anchored the ends of the scale -- 0 impossible, 1 certain, 1/2 even.

vocabulary.definition: A number from 0 to 1 that tells how likely an event is.
An event that can never happen; its probability is 0.
An event that always happens; its probability is 1.
Having the same chance of happening as not; probability 1/2.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'An event has a probability of 1. Impossible, equally likely, or certain?'
Does a probability of 1 mean it never happens, sometimes happens, or always happens?
1 is the very top of the scale -- it always happens -- so the event is certain.
If a student says 'likely,' ask 'is there any chance it does NOT happen at a probability of 1? No -- so it's certain.'
Your turn: a probability of 0 -- which word?

practice_problems.stem: What is the smallest a probability can be? What is the largest?
A probability of 1/2 means the event is ___ likely.
An event has a probability of 0. Classify its likelihood.
The sun will rise tomorrow; its probability is 1. Classify the likelihood.
Rosa classified an event with a probability of 0. Find and fix her mistake.
shown_work: Rosa wrote: 'A probability of 0 means there is a tiny chance, so it could still happen.'
practice_problems.answer: A probability of 0 means it can NEVER happen -- that is impossible, not unlikely. 'Unlikely' is a small chance above 0.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: treating 0 as 'a small chance' instead of no chance.

practice_problems.stem: A spinner is all one color, blue. What is the likelihood of landing on blue?
Describe a real event that is impossible and one that is certain.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: rolling a 7 on a standard number cube is impossible; rolling a number less than 7 is certain.

practice_problems.stem: An event with probability 1/2 and an event with probability 1 -- which is more likely, and why?
practice_problems.answer: The probability-1 event; it is certain, while 1/2 is only an even chance.

activities.title: Impossible, Even, or Certain
activities.instructions:
1. Sort each event card into 'Impossible (0)', 'Equally likely (1/2)', or 'Certain (1)'.
2. For each card, write the probability (0, 1/2, or 1) that matches your choice.
3. Trade piles with another group and check each other's sorts.
4. Debrief: how do you know an event belongs at an END of the scale instead of the middle?

cards.text: Drawing a red marble from a bag of only blue marbles
Rolling a number from 1 to 6 on a standard number cube
Flipping a fair coin and getting heads
Spinning blue on a spinner that is half blue and half red
Rolling a 7 on a standard number cube
The day after Monday being Tuesday

activities.title: Zero Means No Chance
activities.instructions:
1. Read Rosa's claim that a probability of 0 is 'unlikely.'
2. Ask: at a probability of 0, is there ANY chance the event happens?
3. Rewrite the correct classification and explain the word.
4. Write the one-sentence rule for what 0 and 1 mean.

content.worked_problem: An event has a probability of 0. Rosa called it 'unlikely.'
content.error_step: Rosa treated 0 as a small chance above zero.
content.why: A probability of 0 means the event can never happen -- that is impossible. Unlikely is a small chance greater than 0.

strategy_links.why: Anchoring 0 = impossible, 1 = certain, 1/2 = equally likely is a short fact chain choral response makes automatic.
Reversing the endpoints of the scale is a clean, baitable error ideal for find-and-fix.
Thinking aloud 'no chance' for 0 and 'every time' for 1 models the meaning students skip.

questioning_prompts: Does a probability of 0 mean it never happens, or just rarely?
At a probability of 1, is there any chance it does not happen?
What does 1/2 tell you about the chances either way?
Where does this probability sit -- the bottom, the middle, or the top of the scale?
Can a probability ever be more than 1 or less than 0?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reads a probability of 0 as certain or possible, or 1 as unlikely.
misconception_redirects.say: Anchor the ends: 0 means it can NEVER happen (impossible), 1 means it happens EVERY time (certain), and 1/2 is a dead-even chance (equally likely).
misconception_redirects.praise: You anchored the ends of the scale -- 0 impossible, 1 certain, 1/2 even.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student thinks a bigger probability number means less likely.
misconception_redirects.say: On this scale, bigger means MORE likely: 1 is certain at the top, 0 is impossible at the bottom.
misconception_redirects.praise: You read the scale the right direction -- higher is more likely.

quick_checks.prompt: An event has a probability of 0. Impossible, equally likely, or certain?
quick_checks.look_for: Impossible. 'Certain' means the student reversed the endpoints.

quick_checks.prompt: An event has a probability of 1. Classify it.
quick_checks.look_for: Certain. 'Likely' means the student is not anchoring 1 as every-time.

sentence_starters: A probability of ___ means the event ___ happens, so it is ___.

worked_solution.stem: An event has a probability of 0. Classify its likelihood.

steps.annotation: Read the number: this is the very bottom of the 0-to-1 scale.
A probability of 0 means the event can never occur.
Match the value to the word on the scale.

steps.math: check: 0 is the smallest a probability can be
steps.annotation: Confirm 0 anchors the impossible end.

faded_example.stem: An event has a probability of 1. Classify its likelihood.

steps.annotation: Read the number: the very top of the scale.
A probability of 1 means the event always occurs.
Match 'happens every time' to the word on the scale.
Check: is 1 the largest a probability can be?

skills.name: Compute a simple theoretical probability as favorable over total
skills.i_do_script: The probability of an event is the number of favorable outcomes over the total number of equally likely outcomes: favorable over total. Watch a bag with 3 red, 2 blue, and 3 green marbles -- that is 8 in all. The probability of red is the 3 red over the 8 total: 3/8. The bottom is always the total number of outcomes, and the fraction always lands between 0 and 1. If none are favorable it is 0; if all are favorable it is 1.

canonical_error.pattern: Uses a part on the bottom instead of the total, counting only the other outcomes as the whole
canonical_error.example: For 3 red of 8 marbles writes P(red) = 3/5 (red over the other 5) instead of 3/8
canonical_error.why: The student compares favorable to the remaining outcomes (part-to-part) instead of to ALL outcomes. Theoretical probability puts favorable outcomes over the TOTAL number of equally likely outcomes.

skills.item_template: A described bag/spinner/number cube; student computes the probability of an event as favorable/total (fraction). Numeric (fraction) response.

sample_items.stem: A bag has 3 red, 2 blue, and 3 green marbles. What is the probability of drawing a red marble?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3 red over 8 total; 3/5 counts only the non-red as the whole.

sample_items.stem: A spinner has 8 equal sections; 2 are yellow. What is the probability of landing on yellow?
A standard number cube is rolled. What is the probability of rolling a 5?
A bag has 5 green and 7 yellow tiles. What is the probability of drawing a green tile?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 5 green over 12 total; 5/7 puts a part on the bottom.

sample_items.stem: A jar has 6 marbles, all red. What is the probability of drawing a red marble? A blue marble?
A number cube is rolled. What is the probability of rolling an even number (2, 4, or 6)?

redirect_script.stop: What is the TOTAL number of outcomes here?
redirect_script.prompt: Count every outcome to get the bottom number, then put the favorable ones on top: favorable over total. Red over ALL the marbles, not red over the leftovers.
redirect_script.praise: You put favorable over the total -- that's theoretical probability.

vocabulary.definition: Favorable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes.
An outcome that counts as the event you want.
Each outcome has the same chance, like each face of a fair number cube.

worked_example_script.text: Write: a bag has 4 red and 6 blue marbles. What is the probability of red?
How many marbles in all? How many are red?
10 in all, 4 red, so P(red) = 4/10, which reduces to 2/5. The total goes on the bottom.
If a student writes 4/6, ask 'is 6 the total, or just the blue ones? Count all 10.'
Your turn: a number cube -- what is the probability of rolling a 3?

practice_problems.stem: A bag has 10 marbles; 3 are red. What is the total number of marbles?
A spinner has 4 equal sections; 1 is red. What is the probability of red?
A bag has 3 red, 2 blue, and 3 green marbles. Find P(green).
A standard number cube is rolled. Find P(rolling a number greater than 4).
Kai found the probability of drawing red from a bag of 3 red and 5 blue. Find and fix his mistake.
shown_work: Kai wrote: 'There are 3 red and 5 blue.'
practice_problems.answer: Kai put red over blue. The total is 3 + 5 = 8, so P(red) = 3/8, not 3/5.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: part-to-part instead of favorable/total.

practice_problems.stem: A bag has 5 green and 7 yellow tiles. Find P(yellow).
A bag has only red marbles. What is P(red)? What is P(blue)? Explain the 0 and the 1.
Design a spinner with 8 sections so that P(blue) = 1/2. Describe it.
practice_problems.answer: 4 of the 8 sections blue (4/8 = 1/2); any colors for the other 4.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse: build a spinner to a target probability.

activities.title: Favorable Over Total Draw
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a bag-description card (for example, 3 red, 2 blue, 3 green).
2. Write the TOTAL number of marbles first -- that is the denominator.
3. Pick a color and write how many are favorable on top.
4. Write the probability as favorable over total, then reduce if you can.
5. Debrief: what happens to the bottom number if you forget to count the color you are testing?

activities.title: Count the Whole, Not the Rest
activities.instructions:
1. Read Kai's answer that P(red) = 3/5 for a bag of 3 red and 5 blue.
2. Circle every marble that belongs in the total.
3. Redo the probability with the correct denominator.
4. Write the rule for what always goes on the bottom.

content.worked_problem: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue marbles. Kai wrote P(red) = 3/5.
content.error_step: Kai used the 5 blue as the denominator instead of the total.
content.why: The total is 3 + 5 = 8, so P(red) = 3/8. The denominator is every outcome, including the red ones.

strategy_links.why: Using real counters or marbles makes 'favorable over total' concrete before it becomes an abstract fraction.
The part-to-part denominator error is precise and baitable for find-and-fix.
Thinking aloud 'count ALL outcomes for the bottom' models the step students skip.

questioning_prompts: How many outcomes are there in all -- what goes on the bottom?
How many outcomes count as the event you want?
Is your fraction between 0 and 1? It has to be.
Did you put favorable over the total, or over the leftovers?
What would make this probability 0? What would make it 1?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes favorable over the other part instead of over the total.
misconception_redirects.say: Count every outcome to get the bottom number, then put the favorable ones on top: favorable over total. Red over ALL the marbles, not red over the leftovers.
misconception_redirects.praise: You put favorable over the total -- that's theoretical probability.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student leaves the favorable items out of the total.
misconception_redirects.say: The total means EVERY item, including the red ones you are counting on top. 3 red plus 5 blue is 8, not 5.
misconception_redirects.praise: You counted the whole group for the denominator.

quick_checks.prompt: A bag has 2 red and 6 blue. Find P(red).
quick_checks.look_for: 2/8 (or 1/4). An answer of 2/6 means the student used a part, not the total.

quick_checks.prompt: A number cube is rolled. Find P(rolling a 4).
quick_checks.look_for: 1/6. A denominator other than 6 diagnoses a miscounted total.

sentence_starters: There are ___ outcomes in all, and ___ are favorable, so the probability is ___ / ___.

worked_solution.stem: A bag has 4 red, 3 blue, and 1 green marble. What is the probability of drawing a blue marble?

steps.annotation: Count every marble for the denominator.
Count only the outcomes you want for the numerator.
Favorable over total.
A valid probability lands between 0 and 1.

faded_example.stem: A spinner has 10 equal sections; 4 are red. What is the probability of landing on red?

steps.annotation: The whole spinner is the denominator.
Red sections are the numerator.
Write favorable over total, then reduce.
Check the fraction is between 0 and 1.

skills.name: Classify the likelihood of an event described by a spinner or bag
skills.i_do_script: To classify an event from a situation, first find its probability as favorable over total, then place that fraction on the scale. Watch a spinner with 8 equal sections where 1 is red: P(red) = 1/8, which is close to 0, so landing on red is UNLIKELY. If 4 of the 8 were red, P(red) = 4/8 = 1/2, so it would be equally likely. The count alone does not tell you -- 1 red out of 8 is unlikely, but 1 red out of 2 would be equally likely.

canonical_error.pattern: Classifies by the raw count of favorable outcomes instead of the probability out of the total
canonical_error.example: Says landing on red is 'likely' because there are 6 red sections, ignoring that there are 20 sections in all (6/20 is unlikely)
canonical_error.why: The student judges by how many favorable outcomes there are, not the fraction of the whole. Likelihood depends on the probability (favorable over total), so the denominator matters as much as the count.

skills.item_template: A described spinner/bag/number cube; student finds the probability and classifies it as impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, or certain. Multiple choice.

sample_items.stem: A spinner has 8 equal sections; 1 is red. The spinner is spun once. How likely is landing on red?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1/8 is close to 0; 'likely' ignores the total of 8.

sample_items.stem: A bag has 6 red and 6 blue marbles. How likely is drawing a red marble?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Half the marbles are red -- an even chance.

sample_items.stem: A bag has 7 green and 1 white tile. How likely is drawing a green tile?
A spinner has 5 equal sections, all blue. How likely is landing on blue?

redirect_script.stop: How many sections in all -- what is the probability out of the total?
redirect_script.prompt: Don't judge by the count alone. Find the probability as favorable over total first, THEN place it: close to 0 is unlikely, 1/2 is even, close to 1 is likely.
redirect_script.praise: You classified by the probability, not just the count -- the total matters.

vocabulary.definition: How probable an event is, described in words like unlikely or likely.
A small chance; a probability close to 0 but not 0.
A large chance; a probability close to 1 but not 1.
An outcome or set of outcomes you are asking about, like landing on red.

worked_example_script.text: Write: a bag has 2 red and 10 blue marbles. How likely is drawing red?
What is P(red) as favorable over total? Is that close to 0, 1/2, or 1?
P(red) = 2/12 = 1/6, which is close to 0, so drawing red is unlikely.
If a student says 'likely because there are 2 reds,' ask '2 out of how many? 2 of 12 is a small chance.'
Your turn: a spinner with 8 sections, 4 red -- how likely is red?

practice_problems.stem: A spinner has 4 sections; 2 are red. What is P(red)?
Is a probability of 1/8 close to 0 or close to 1?
A spinner has 8 equal sections; 1 is red. How likely is red?
A bag has 7 green and 1 white tile. How likely is green?
Nina classified drawing red from a bag of 6 red and 14 blue. Find and fix her mistake.
shown_work: Nina wrote: 'There are 6 red -- that is a lot.'
practice_problems.answer: Nina used the count, not the probability. P(red) = 6/20 = 3/10, which is close to 0, so red is UNLIKELY, not likely.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: classifying by count instead of favorable/total.

practice_problems.stem: A bag has 5 red and 5 blue marbles. How likely is red?
Describe a bag of marbles for which drawing red is unlikely but drawing blue is likely.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: 1 red and 7 blue (P(red) = 1/8 unlikely, P(blue) = 7/8 likely).
practice_problems.notes: Reverse: build a situation to targets.

practice_problems.stem: Spinner A has 2 red of 4 sections; Spinner B has 2 red of 8. Landing on red is a different likelihood on each -- explain.
practice_problems.answer: A: 2/4 = 1/2 equally likely; B: 2/8 = 1/4 unlikely. Same count of red, different totals.
practice_problems.notes: Shows the denominator drives the classification.

materials: Likelihood-word cards (impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, certain) plus decoys
activities.instructions:
1. For each situation card, find its probability as favorable over total.
2. Match it to the correct likelihood word.
3. Two likelihood cards are decoys that match nothing -- set them aside and say why.
4. Debrief: which situations were tempting to classify by the count instead of the probability?

pairs.left: A bag with 6 red and 6 blue marbles
A bag with 7 green and 1 white tile

activities.title: Count Isn't Chance
activities.instructions:
1. Read Nina's claim that 6 red out of 20 makes red 'likely.'
2. Compute the actual probability of red.
3. Place that probability on the scale (close to 0, 1/2, or 1).
4. Write the rule: classify by the ____, not by the count.

content.worked_problem: A bag has 6 red and 14 blue. Nina said drawing red is likely because there are 6 reds.
content.error_step: Nina judged by the count of red instead of the probability.
content.why: P(red) = 6/20 = 3/10, close to 0, so red is unlikely. The total of 20 makes 6 a small share.

strategy_links.why: Pairs debate 'count versus probability' and must justify each classification, surfacing the misconception.
The count-not-probability error is precise and baitable for find-and-fix.

questioning_prompts: What is the probability of this event as favorable over total?
Is that fraction close to 0, at 1/2, or close to 1?
Would the answer change if there were more sections in all?
Are you judging by the count or by the probability?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student classifies by the number of favorable outcomes, ignoring the total.
misconception_redirects.say: Don't judge by the count alone. Find the probability as favorable over total first, THEN place it: close to 0 is unlikely, 1/2 is even, close to 1 is likely.
misconception_redirects.praise: You classified by the probability, not just the count -- the total matters.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls any fraction under 1/2 'impossible' or any fraction over 1/2 'certain.'
misconception_redirects.say: Save 'impossible' for exactly 0 and 'certain' for exactly 1. In between, use unlikely, equally likely, or likely.
misconception_redirects.praise: You reserved impossible and certain for the ends and used the middle words correctly.

quick_checks.prompt: A spinner has 10 sections, 1 red. How likely is red?
quick_checks.look_for: Unlikely (1/10). 'Likely' means the student judged by the single red count.

quick_checks.prompt: A bag has 4 red and 4 blue. How likely is red?
quick_checks.look_for: Equally likely (1/2). Anything else means the student did not compute the probability.

sentence_starters: P(event) = ___ / ___ = ___, which is close to ___, so the event is ___.
There are ___ outcomes in all and ___ favorable, so this event is ___.

worked_solution.stem: A bag has 3 red and 9 blue marbles. How likely is drawing a red marble?

skills.name: Classify a fraction probability on the full likelihood scale
skills.i_do_script: When a probability is given as a fraction, I place it on the scale by comparing it to 0, 1/2, and 1. If it is close to 0 (but not 0), the event is unlikely; if it equals 1/2, it is equally likely; if it is close to 1 (but not 1), it is likely. Watch: 1/6 is about 0.17, close to 0, so it is unlikely. 5/6 is about 0.83, close to 1, so it is likely. 1/2 sits exactly in the middle -- equally likely. I compare the whole fraction to the benchmark 1/2, not just the numbers in it.

canonical_error.pattern: Judges the fraction by a single number (numerator or denominator) instead of its value compared to 1/2
canonical_error.example: Calls 1/8 'likely' because 8 is big, or calls 7/8 'unlikely' because the numerator is small, instead of comparing each to 1/2
canonical_error.why: The student reads one part of the fraction as 'the size' rather than evaluating the whole fraction. Likelihood depends on how close the value is to 0, 1/2, or 1 -- so you must compare the fraction to the benchmark 1/2.

skills.item_template: A probability given as a fraction; student classifies it as impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, or certain. Multiple choice.

sample_items.stem: An event has a probability of 1/6. How likely is it?

sample_items.distractor_logic: Exactly the middle of the scale.

sample_items.stem: An event has a probability of 7/8. How likely is it?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 7/8 = 0.875, close to 1; a small numerator does not make it unlikely.

redirect_script.stop: Is this fraction closer to 0, to 1/2, or to 1?
redirect_script.prompt: Compare the whole fraction to 1/2. If it is below 1/2 it is unlikely, at 1/2 it is equally likely, above 1/2 it is likely. Turn it into a decimal if that helps: 1/8 = 0.125.
redirect_script.praise: You compared the fraction to 1/2 -- that's how you place it on the scale.

vocabulary.definition: The order impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, certain from probability 0 to 1.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'An event has a probability of 3/4. How likely is it?'
Is 3/4 below 1/2, equal to 1/2, or above 1/2?

If a student says 'unlikely because the top is only 3,' ask 'is 3/4 more or less than 1/2? It is more.'

activities.title: Where on the Scale?
activities.instructions:
1. Sort each fraction into 'Unlikely (below 1/2)', 'Equally likely (1/2)', or 'Likely (above 1/2)'.
2. Before sorting, turn each fraction into a decimal and write it on the card.
3. Line the 'unlikely' and 'likely' piles up in order from nearest to 1/2 to farthest.
4. Debrief: how did comparing to 1/2 settle the close calls?

activities.title: Don't Judge by One Number
activities.instructions:
1. Read Theo's claim that 1/8 is 'likely' because 8 is big.
2. Turn 1/8 into a decimal.
3. Compare it to 1/2 and reclassify it.
4. Write the rule about what you must compare -- the whole fraction, not one number.

content.worked_problem: An event has a probability of 1/8. Theo called it 'likely' because the denominator is big.
content.error_step: Theo judged by the denominator 8 instead of the value of the fraction.
content.why: 1/8 = 0.125, well below 1/2, so it is unlikely. A bigger denominator with a numerator of 1 makes the probability SMALLER.

strategy_links.why: Number talks on friendly fractions (1/8, 1/2, 7/8) build the sense of closeness to 0, 1/2, and 1.
The judge-by-one-number error is clean and baitable for find-and-fix.
A 0-to-1 number line makes 'compare to 1/2' a visual placement instead of a rule to memorize.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls a small-but-nonzero probability 'impossible' or a large-but-under-1 probability 'certain.'

skills.name: Compare the likelihood of events given their probabilities
skills.i_do_script: To compare two events, I compare their probabilities: the event with the probability CLOSER TO 1 is more likely. Watch: the probability of Sam hiking 5 miles is 5/8 and Joe's is 3/8. 5/8 = 0.625 and 3/8 = 0.375, so Sam's is closer to 1 -- Sam is more likely. If the probabilities are equal, the events are equally likely. Comparing fractions with the same denominator is easy: the bigger numerator is more likely. With different denominators, turn them into decimals.

canonical_error.pattern: Picks the event with the bigger denominator or 'bigger-looking' number instead of the larger probability
canonical_error.example: Given P = 1/4 versus 1/3, picks 1/4 as more likely because 4 > 3, when 1/3 is about 0.33, larger than 1/4 = 0.25
canonical_error.why: The student compares a single part of each fraction instead of the actual probability values. To compare likelihoods, compare the probabilities themselves -- the one closer to 1 is more likely -- which for a shared numerator means a SMALLER denominator is more likely.

skills.item_template: Two or more events with given probabilities; student picks the most (or least) likely, or judges them equal. Multiple choice.

sample_items.stem: The probability Sam hikes 5 miles is 5/8; the probability Joe does is 3/8. Who is more likely?

sample_items.answer: Event B (1/3 is about 0.33, greater than 1/4 = 0.25)
sample_items.distractor_logic: The bigger denominator (4) is actually the smaller probability.

sample_items.stem: Event A has probability 2/5 and Event B has probability 2/5. Which is more likely?

redirect_script.prompt: Compare the probabilities, not one number in each. Turn them into decimals if the denominators differ: the value closer to 1 is more likely. With the same top number, a smaller bottom is more likely.
redirect_script.praise: You compared the actual probabilities -- closer to 1 wins.

vocabulary.definition: Having a probability closer to 1 than another event's.
Decide which probability is larger, using decimals or a common denominator.
Two events with the same probability.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'P(A) = 3/4 and P(B) = 2/3. Which event is more likely?'
What is each probability as a decimal? Which is closer to 1?
3/4 = 0.75 and 2/3 = about 0.67, so A (0.75) is closer to 1 -- Event A is more likely.
If a student picks B because 3 < 4 somewhere, ask 'which decimal is bigger, 0.75 or 0.67?'

practice_problems.stem: Mia compared events with probabilities 1/6 and 1/4. Find and fix her mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Mia compared the denominators. 1/6 is about 0.17 and 1/4 = 0.25, so 1/4 is more likely. With the same top number, the SMALLER denominator is more likely.

practice_problems.answer: A -- 2/3 is about 0.667 versus 5/8 = 0.625, so A is closer to 1.

practice_problems.stem: Write probabilities for two events so the first is more likely, even though its numerator is smaller. Explain.

activities.title: Probability War
materials: Deck of probability cards (fractions between 0 and 1)
activities.instructions:
1. Split the deck evenly between the two players.
2. Each player flips one card at the same time.
3. The card with the probability CLOSER TO 1 wins both cards; convert to decimals if you disagree.
4. If the two probabilities are equal, it is a tie -- each keeps their card.
5. Debrief: name a hand where a bigger denominator LOST -- why?

activities.title: Bigger Bottom, Smaller Chance
activities.instructions:
1. Read Mia's claim that 1/6 is more likely than 1/4 because 6 > 4.
2. Turn both fractions into decimals.
3. Decide which probability is closer to 1 and fix the comparison.
4. Write the rule about the denominator when the top numbers match.

content.worked_problem: Compare probabilities 1/6 and 1/4. Mia said 1/6 is more likely because 6 > 4.
content.error_step: Mia compared the denominators instead of the probabilities.
content.why: 1/6 is about 0.17 and 1/4 = 0.25, so 1/4 is more likely. With the same numerator, a bigger denominator is a smaller probability.

strategy_links.why: Pairs argue which event is more likely and must justify with the probabilities, exposing the denominator error.
The bigger-denominator comparison error is clean and baitable for find-and-fix.
A journal note on why a bigger denominator can mean a smaller chance consolidates the comparison rule.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4 (classify a fraction probability on the scale) -- the At-proficiency core of the standard. If they pass, push to S5 (compare two probabilities). If they fail, drop to S1 to check whether the three anchors (0, 1/2, 1) are solid. S2 (compute favorable/total) and S3 (classify from a situation) branch off the core as the supporting number-building steps.
